Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Sarah Rogers, the state department’s undersecretary for public diplomacy, provided the so-called ‘GEC files’ to Jennica Pounds, a rightwing online data analyst known as DataRepublican. Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty Images Trump administration Documents leaked by Trump official to bolster a conspiracy show ‘absolutely nothing’ Inside the US state department, critics are still attacking a shuttered office established to counter foreign propaganda. Now, some of its work is also being resumed Joseph Gedeon in Washington Sun 30 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 06.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A botched leak of purportedly explosive government files to a prominent conservative online personality was supposed to offer proof of what the Trump administration and its allies have long alleged: that a little-known office inside the US state department, created to fight foreign propaganda, had secretly become a tool for domestic censorship. Two former high-ranking officials at the Global Engagement Center (GEC), a target of Republican ire that lost its funding in 2024 and was disbanded after Donald Trump ’s return to office in 2025, say the documents show nothing of the kind. Instead, they argue, the files are a symptom of a protracted and bitter political fight over an office that spent nearly a decade tracking and countering foreign influence operations, particularly from Russia, China and Iran. Trump administration shutters US office countering foreign disinformation Read more And the state department is now resuming some of this work in other parts of its operation, including plans – laid out in a proposal reviewed by the Guardian – to pay social media influencers across south-east Asia as part of an $11m campaign to counter Chinese propaganda. Sarah Rogers, the state epartment’s undersecretary for public diplomacy, provided the so-called “GEC files” to Jennica Pounds, a rightwing online data analyst known as DataRepublican – only for Pounds to claim earlier this month she was leaked the documents as part of a bid to “entrap” her. Rogers, who denied this claim, then published the files herself, claiming officials inside the center “betrayed their stated mission”. The files included a 2022 GEC report on “gendered disinformation”, a flashpoint in the culture wars. “These guys have consistently misrepresented what the GEC did, and this was a great example of that,” said Daniel Kimmage, who served as the center’s principal deputy coordinator and acting coordinator from its founding in 2017 until its complete dissolution in 2025. His own congressional testimony was included in the leaked files. Kimmage and Carrie Goux, a Joe Biden appointee and the center’s former acting deputy coordinator, say nothing in the material shows the GEC, whose mandate was explicitly foreign-facing, ever turned its tools on Americans. “If the smoking gun was a gendered disinformation report, that feels like they came up short,” Goux said. “There seems to be absolutely nothing here.” Weaponization The dispute is the latest chapter in a years-long campaign by conservatives to portray the GEC as part of a broader effort by the US government and technology companies to suppress rightwing speech. Republican congressmen including Michael McCaul, former chair of the House foreign affairs committee, argued in a July 2024 letter that the GEC was “at best indifferent to, and at worst complicit in” stretching the definition of disinformation to “censor” conservative speech in the US. Trump’s return to the presidency drew this view into the heart of the federal government. The center was abolished in 2025 , and what remained of its work scattered across the state department. Much of that Republican-led campaign centered on how the GEC had funded the Global Disinformation Index (GDI), a UK-based non-profit that rates media outlets by how likely they are to spread disinformation, to help monitor propaganda in Asia. But in 2022 the GDI separately published its own study of the US media market that rated several conservative outlets, including Newsmax, One America News and the New York Post, as high-risk – a finding its critics have cited ever since as evidence that a foreign-facing office had funded a group meddling in domestic politics. The question raised by the files leaked this month is narrower, however: whether they show the GEC itself ran a domestic censorship operation. Kimmage and Goux insist they do not. Kimmage said his own congressional testimony, which Rogers included in the leak, had been selectively read. “If you look at the transcript, [the question was], ‘Does GEC take positions on US outlets?’ And I said, ‘No, it didn’t,’” he said. Rogers “tried to twist that into something that it wasn’t”, according to Kimmage. “For people who talk a lot about weaponization of government, this seems a lot closer to the weaponization of government and psy-opping of the American people than anything that the emails from the Global Engagement Center show.” ‘False’ allegations Pounds, the rightwing analyst, is not a neutral bystander. Days after the documents were released, she disclosed that she had been quietly working since July as a special government employee for the defense department. On Friday, Pounds released a database to track US citizens in the Democratic Socialists of America. The Pentagon did not respond when asked whether the database is included in her scope of government work. Both former senior officials, Kimmage and Goux, draw a sharp line between the accusations made by critics of the GEC and what the center actually did. “We were not ever looking at Americans,” Goux said. “We were looking at the foreign actors and what their [tactics, techniques and procedures] … are doing overseas.” US directs embassies to team up against foreign ‘hostility’ – and use X to ‘counter anti-American propaganda’ Read more The GEC “did what its congressional mandate charged it to do, which is to fight foreign [misinformation and] disinformation”, added Kimmage. “This allegation that it’s censoring Americans is false.” During its almost decade-long existence, the center published eight detailed public reports on Russian and Chinese information operations and ran four major exposures of Russian disinformation campaigns – in Latin America, Africa and Moldova, and on the Kremlin-linked network RT. Its largest such operation traced a Kremlin-backed effort called the “ African Initiative ”, which the center said had recruited local journalists, bloggers and public figures to spread conspiracy theories about US-funded health programs across the continent. In January 2024, the GEC helped broker an international pact on countering foreign state disinformation that eventually drew more than two dozen government signatories, among them Moldova, Spain, Estonia, Poland and Finland – a framework its backers hoped other countries would use to build their own version of the office. A 2022 inspector general review found the GEC “generally effective” at supporting counter-disinformation programs overall, while flagging weaknesses in its internal controls, contractor oversight and strategic planning. That record was enough to sustain bipartisan support: senators Rob Portman, a Republican, and Chris Murphy, a Democrat, repeatedly pushed to fund and strengthen the center, and its authorization survived multiple renewal fights before House Republicans, increasingly focused on the domestic-speech question, declined to extend it again in 2024. That mandate cost roughly $61m per year. The GEC employed about 120 people before Congress declined to reauthorize it, letting the office lapse at the end of 2024. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio , later folded what remained of its work into a new counter foreign information manipulation and interference office, framing the closure as an end to wasteful, censorious government overreach. Trust exercise Now, less than a year after the GEC shut down, a proposal reviewed by the Guardian shows the state department preparing to pay up to 30 online influencers across 11 countries in south-east Asia $2,500 apiece as part of an $11m, multi-year campaign to counter Chinese propaganda. The project, which would be operated by the US Mission to USEAN, has three parts: a $5m messaging campaign, a $3m program training influencers and journalists to counter Chinese propaganda, and a $3m trip bringing about 180 participants to studios in Washington and Houston “for intensive collaboration, studio production and first-hand engagement with US institutions and creators”. The proposal’s planning materials describe the ideal recruit as starting from a “welcoming” position of what one document calls the “rejecting-affirming continuum”: someone not yet sold on the US, but not hostile either. As participants move through the accelerator, the materials say, exposure to evidence of US commitment in the region and training in spotting propaganda from China (which has reportedly invested billions of dollars in disinformation efforts globally) is meant to carry them toward the “affirming” end of that scale, publicly backing closer ties with Washington on trade, tech standards and the South China Sea. The document cited the rightwing analyst and new Pentagon special government employee, Jennica Pounds, the DataRepublican, as an ideal model to seek out in other recruits abroad. Contacted for comment, the state department declined to directly address questions about the documents released by Rogers, the influencer proposal, the department’s current foreign influence programs and whether other regions are being targeted as well. A state department official said: “Undersecretary Rogers has been clear that the department will continue to confront censorship, anti-American propaganda and coercive influence directly while demonstrating the enduring advantages of freedom, accountability and open communication.” Meanwhile, the office of policy, planning and resources for public diplomacy (R/PPR) was separately shopping for commercial help with a similar mission this spring. A government filing from May 2026 shows the R/PPR requesting information from vendors on software that can mine open-source data, map “adversarial propaganda influence networks” and detect deepfakes. That apparent contradiction is not lost on the GEC’s former staff. “Are they trying to re-create it? Probably,” Goux said. “But now they’re spending a lot more tax dollars doing that, trying to get contractors to do some of the stuff that we were doing.” Goux put the broader cost in plainer terms still. “The US has lost their seat at the table to do that, and that’s unfortunate,” she said. “I hope we can gain it back, but we’re losing trust too, and that’s significant.” Explore more on these topics Trump administration Republicans Marco Rubio Donald Trump US Congress US foreign policy US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.politico.eu/article/inside-k.text: Kaja Kallas, the EU’s chief diplomat, is leading a fierce behind-the-scenes push against Franco-German plans to overhaul her diplomatic service — courting capitals and using a new secretary-general to develop alternative reform plans. Kallas’ campaign involves convincing EU governments that the bloc’s foreign-policy problems stem from unanimous decision-making rules and poor implementation of its treaties — not from the current institutional setup, according to three EU officials informed of her plans. They were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive internal strategy. The fight comes as the 15-year-old European External Action Service faces criticism that it is no longer fit for purpose at a moment when Russia’s war against Ukraine, Donald Trump’s demands on Europe, conflict in the Middle East and a more confrontational China are all testing the bloc’s ability to act abroad. The Commission is also expanding its role in foreign policy, while Berlin is pressing to cut EU operating costs amid negotiations over the bloc’s next long-term budget. Advertisement Advertisement Kallas’ allies fear that an overhaul intended to make EU foreign policy more effective could instead give President Ursula von der Leyen’s Commission greater control over the work overseen by the high representative. “If I have somebody above me who is actually deciding, then it doesn’t work,” Kallas told journalists Wednesday after a debate with EU foreign ministers in Wicklow, Ireland. One diplomat, referring to the Franco-German plans, said: “She [Kallas] wants to delay the whole process because she doesn’t want to be subject to von der Leyen.” Another said “she wants this whole thing to go away.” The pushback is taking shape through Kajsa Ollongren, the EEAS’ new secretary-general, who has been touring EU capitals to discuss reform proposals with national governments. Ollongren will brief staff on the findings from that tour at a town hall meeting with the EEAS this week, where Kallas will formally introduce her, according to the officials and an EU diplomat. Ollongren is also expected to propose the creation of a “council of elders” task force to reflect on possible internal reforms, one of the officials said. Advertisement Advertisement The group would include the EEAS’ former secretary-general, Belén Martínez Carbonell, who has delayed taking up a new role as head of the EU delegation in Mexico to advise Ollongren. Senior EEAS official Charles Fries is also set to contribute, according to the officials and the diplomat. The push seeks to give the EEAS more control over a reform debate that could determine whether the service remains a distinct part of the EU’s foreign policy machinery or becomes more closely integrated into the Commission. The Franco-German plans, set out in a paper seen by POLITICO, include moving much of the EEAS staff into the EU executive. Although they call for reinforcing Kallas’ formal role, her allies see them potentially allowing von der Leyen’s Commission to take greater control of foreign policy. Kajsa Ollongren, who has been touring EU capitals to discuss reform proposals with national governments, making a statement during a meeting of NATO defense ministers in Brussels in June 2024. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images The EEAS currently straddles the Council and the Commission: Kallas works with national governments in the Council, where foreign policy decisions are made, while the service coordinates with the Commission on its external-facing work. Kallas signaled her concern about the plans on Wednesday, saying a “majority” of EU foreign ministers had opposed the institutional change. In recent days, in addition to the Franco-German discussion paper on the EEAS, 11 capitals including Paris and Berlin signed an open letter to Kallas calling for more efficient decision-making in EU foreign policy . Advertisement Advertisement The letter opens the door to the selective use of qualified majority voting for foreign and security policy decisions. Currently, any decision on topics under those headings requires unanimous backing — leading to major bottlenecks under former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who opposed the bloc’s support for Ukraine. While agreeing with the aim of making EU foreign policy faster-moving and better able to protect the bloc’s interests, Kallas argued Wednesday that the solution is to enforce EU treaties and legal texts that, in theory, give her oversight of the Commission’s external-facing policy units without requiring big reforms. “The problem is not the treaties, the institutional setup,” she said. “The problem is the implementation.” CORRECTION: A previous version of this article misstated the names of Kajsa Ollongren and Belén Martínez Carbonell.

https://www.dw.com/en/g7-ministers-meet-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PEKO Prefer DW on Google The G7 meeting coincides with US-mediated talks between Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi scheduled to begin on Tuesday [FILE: March 13, 2024] Image: Andriy Andriyenko/SOPA Images/Sipa USA/picture alliance Advertisement Foreign ministers from the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrialized nations are set to meet in Paris on Monday and Tuesday for talks on how Europe can be part of US efforts to end Russia’s war on Ukraine and how to urge Washington to not resume military action against Iran. The meeting will bring together leading diplomats from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. It coincides with US-mediated talks between Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi scheduled to begin on Tuesday. European governments are concerned the US might be pushing Ukraine to a settlement favoring Russia . US President Donald Trump, in the run-up to the Abu Dhabi talks, said a "very big" deal was in the making , suggesting Ukraine could emerge from a settlement with altered ‌borders. "I think we're gonna have it done, and I think it's ‌gonna happen ​and they're gonna end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine," Trump told broadcaster CBS. The US president also said the deal would involve all of Europe. European leaders fear that Putin may have too much influence over the Trump administration Image: Dmitry Azarov/Kommersant Photo/Sipa USA/picture alliance Europe insists it's at the table About the talks in Abu Dhabi, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told RTL radio that "Europeans will be represented and France will participate in these talks." European leaders have long insisted that any deal to end the war should include the continent's participation in the talks and that any settlement should not come at the expense of Ukraine's sovereignty. When asked about the US plans for a possible agreement to end the war in Ukraine, Barrot said he did not know the details but stressed that no deal affecting the European security architecture could be done without the Europeans. Particular attention at the upcoming meeting will be on US Secretary of State Marco Rubio who will attend both days unlike the last G7 meeting where he came only for one. Rubio suggested that recent discussions had made progress on security guarantees for Ukraine and the wider European region. Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner has also described US efforts to develop a broader European security framework. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has in the past expressed doubts over proposals for a new European security framework, suggesting that any such debates should follow, rather than precede, efforts to end the war. What Trump’s Russia talks could cost Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video US strategy on Iran remains unclear The G7 ministers are also expected to discuss US tensions with Iran, as Trump has not ruled out additional military strikes against the country. Washington has previously considered targeting suspected nuclear facilities, including the site known as Pickaxe Mountain, following the US midterm elections last week. Tehran denies that the location is a nuclear facility. European governments are seeking a diplomatic resolution rather than a resumption of military action. Global attention is particularly on the restoration of normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for international energy supplies. Trump recently said that Iranian officials were keen to reach an agreement, suggesting negotiations remained possible . The Paris gathering is among the final major diplomatic events of France's G7 presidency. The United States is scheduled to assume the group's rotating presidency in 2027.
